Centcom sets up 'Task Force Iron Gate' to disrupt Iran’s weapons transfers

The United States Central Command (Centcom) has directed the establishment of a task force that will support US government's efforts to prevent Iran from using ground routes to transport advanced weapons and other materials.

In a statement issued on Saturday on X, Centcom said Admiral Brad Cooper has directed the formation of Task Force Iron Gate, an internal staff of approximately 20 civilian and military personnel based in Tampa, Florida.

It will coordinate with other US government agencies on preventing the movement of advanced weapons systems, dual-use technologies, sanctioned materials, and "illegal revenue streams" across Iran's land borders and the Caspian Sea, Centcom added.

"The establishment of Task Force Iron Gate reinforces the success of our ironclad blockade against Iran at sea," said Cooper. "Strengthening CENTCOM's collaboration with U.S. inter-agency partners will further constrain Iran's ability to finance terrorism, rebuild weapons factories, and replenish their military."

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Paraguay's pro-Israel former president taken into custody over banking crisis
item.description:
Paraguay's pro-Israel former president taken into custody over banking crisis

Paraguayan prosecutors charged pro-Israel ex-president Santiago Pena and took him into custody Saturday over a banking crisis that saw millions cut off from their money and sparked major protests.

Pena, Paraguay's youngest-ever president, was removed from office by the Senate on Friday, just three days after the collapse of a leading bank with which he had business links.

An indictment against Pena states that "between 2023 and 2026, UENO BANK S.A. allegedly received deposits and loans from public and pension entities" and that it "was also allegedly granting loans to companies linked to the bank's economic group in an irregular manner."

The 47-year-old economist owned shares in Ueno Holding, the controlling company of the bank, until he sold them last year.

Pena maintained close relations with Israel, and in 2024, reopened his country’s embassy in the occupied Jerusalem, making it the sixth country at the time to make the move. 

Pena's removal is a further blow for US President Donald Trump's network of allies in South America.

Trump's favourite for Brazilian president, Flavio Bolsonaro, was defeated by left-wing incumbent Lula Inacio Lula da Silva last month.

Report by AFP

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Iran tells Russia talks with US without guarantees won't end conflict, report says
item.description:
Iran tells Russia talks with US without guarantees won't end conflict, report says

Iran’s ambassador to Moscow Kazem Jalali has said Iran and Russia have discussed strengthening military and security cooperation, with Tehran stressing that talks with the US could not end the conflict without credible guarantees, according to Mehr News Agency.

Jalali said that during a three-hour meeting, Major General Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, briefed Russian President Vladimir Putin on Tehran’s strategic priorities, including accelerating construction of the Rasht-Astara railway and completing the International North-South Transport Corridor (INSTC).

Jalali said Rezaei conveyed Tehran’s position that negotiations with Washington could not end the conflict without credible guarantees, citing repeated "US violations of commitments" during previous diplomatic engagements, Mehr reported.

He said Rezaei also explained Iran’s response to a letter from US Vice President JD Vance, stressing that dialogue alone could not provide a basis for ending the war.

According to Jalali, Rezaei cited several instances in which Iran had come under attack during diplomatic initiatives, including negotiations in Oman and Geneva, as well as engagements surrounding the Islamabad MoU.

The ambassador said Tehran had made acceptance of its seven strategic conditions by Washington a prerequisite for any new diplomatic initiative. He added that Moscow understood Iran’s position and agreed that commitments had to be implemented.

item.description:
Saudi Aramco building in Riyadh damaged by falling debris in attempted attack, ministry says

An administrative building belonging to state oil giant Saudi Aramco in Riyadh was damaged by falling debris following an attempted attack on Sunday, with no injuries or fatalities reported, the kingdom's Energy Ministry said.

A witness told Reuters that they saw blown-out windows across several floors of the Aramco Tower, one of the tallest buildings in the capital's King Abdullah Financial District.

The incident, which the ministry said caused limited damage, came after the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted two missiles fired by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis towards Riyadh.

Aramco was not immediately available for comment, and there was no immediate statement from the Houthis.

Multiple loud booms were heard in Riyadh earlier on Sunday, a Reuters witness said, shortly after Saudi Civil Defense issued an early-warning alert of a potential threat in the region. Authorities later announced that the danger had passed.

The Saudi-led coalition subsequently said it had intercepted and destroyed two cruise missiles in Riyadh and the kingdom's southern region.

Reporting by Reuters

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] France's polarised road to 2027: Repression, racism and the rise of the far right
item.description:
France's polarised road to 2027: Repression, racism and the rise of the far right

Submitted by Tassa Adidi on Fri, 11/06/2026 - 14:36
With protests curbed, minorities targeted and the left delegitimised, the mainstreaming of far-right ideas is bringing Marine Le Pen closer than ever to power
Protesters display a banner reading "Racism kills, We stand in solidarity with the city of Trappes" during a demonstration as part of a nationwide day of actions in Marseille, France, 5 November 2026 (Justine Meddah/AFP)
Off

Grief and anger filled the streets of Trappes, north of Paris, on 30 October as thousands paid tribute to the victims of a racist attack committed a week earlier. A 26-year-old Black man, Pengo Bossio Wangi, was killed and seven other people injured, including a 12-year-old girl.

Placed in pre-trial detention, the suspect, 39-year-old Kevin Tessier, admitted that he had specifically targeted people whom he described as "Muslim, African or North African". Investigators found in his home a copy of Mein Kampf and self-made stickers referencing the National Rally (RN), the far-right party of 2027 presidential candidate Marine Le Pen.

According to Trappes mayor Ali Rabeh, the suspect's "hatred did not come from nowhere. It was planted in his mind through the constant repetition of words and narratives that turned these minorities into targets to be eliminated".

Rabeh directly blamed the RN and its president, Jordan Bardella, who described Trappes in 2022 as "a miniature Islamic republic".

The mayor also criticised politicians who, "within the republican camp, thought it wise to appease the far right by adopting its language, flirting with its ideas and even enshrining its demands into law".

Rabeh further condemned the role of the CNews channel and the "media empire" of conservative businessman Vincent Bollore, calling on independent media to "hold the line" and to "stop giving airtime to convicted racists".

One of them is Eric Zemmour, leader of the far-right Reconquete! party and a potential candidate in the 2027 presidential race. Convicted several times for incitement to hatred and discrimination, Zemmour accused "hordes of Arab and African barbarians" of organising looting during recent demonstrations over living standards and conditions in schools and universities.

He was not alone. Figures from the National Rally, right-wing presidential candidate Bruno Retailleau, and even the government's spokesperson blamed suburban "thugs" for the unrest. Former Prime Minister Edouard Philippe, also a presidential hopeful, spoke of an "overrepresentation of French people from immigrant backgrounds among the rioters".

It was precisely these racialised communities from the banlieues - France’s working‑class, often ethnically diverse suburbs - that Tessier chose to attack. He told police he had targeted them to "avenge looted shopkeepers" and said he had chosen Trappes because, like Bardella, he considered the town "a stronghold of Islamists".

‘The normalisation of far-right discourse’

For Dominique Sopo, president of SOS Racisme, discriminatory rhetoric targeting residents of banlieues helps explain the motives behind the Trappes attack.

"The recurring dehumanisation of people perceived as Arab, Black or Muslim, combined with the biased media coverage of the recent demonstrations, plays a direct role in pushing criminals to commit violent acts," he told Middle East Eye.

"Portraying part of the population as 'thugs' or an 'existential threat' inevitably legitimises violent behaviour in the minds of certain individuals," he added, warning that other racist attacks could occur in the run-up to the presidential election.

‘The recurring dehumanisation of people perceived as Arab, Black or Muslim, combined with the biased media coverage of the recent demonstrations, plays a direct role in pushing criminals to commit violent acts’

- Dominique Sopo, president of SOS Racisme

Since 2022, eight people in France have been killed by far-right activists because of their perceived ethnicity or immigrant background. Among the most recent victims were Djamel Bendjaballah, killed in Dunkirk in 2024 by a member of the ultra-right French Patriotic Brigade (BFP), and Hichem Miraoui, who was murdered in the Var region in 2025 by a neighbour sympathetic to the National Rally because he was Arab.

Despite calls from organisations such as SOS Racisme, the BFP has not been formally dissolved. Since the beginning of Emmanuel Macron's presidency, only around 20 far-right identity groups have been banned, despite an estimated 300 operating across the country.

In recent weeks, such groups have organised targeted assaults on the sidelines of demonstrations in several French cities, claiming to be "defending businesses".

According to Le Monde, some of their attacks on demonstrators took place in full view of riot police. Rather than arresting the perpetrators, officers allegedly restrained the victims and allowed the attackers to leave.

In recent days, civil society groups and media outlets have also revealed online exchanges in which individuals threatened to ambush racialised delivery workers, poison halal food in supermarkets and target Muslims during street prayers outside mosques.

In Paris on 31 October, graffiti promoting "remigration" - the mass deportation of immigrants - was also discovered on the fronts of several shops. That day, a conference organised by the ultra right on the same theme was ultimately banned by the authorities.

The concept of remigration is closely linked to the far-right "Great Replacement" conspiracy theory. France's junior minister for combating discrimination, Aurore Berge, recently sparked controversy by refusing to describe it as racist.

For Abdellali Hajjat, a sociology professor at the Free University of Brussels, such positions contribute to "the normalisation of far-right discourse".

"When members of the government embrace myths - not theories - such as the 'Great Replacement', 'Brotherism', or 'Islamo-leftism', they legitimise an entire racist and conspiratorial worldview," he told MEE.

"Brotherism" or "Entryism", presented as a strategy of political infiltration by the Muslim Brotherhood, was the subject of a Senate bill in May, while "Islamo-leftism" - the alleged convergence of parts of the political left with Islamist interests - has been invoked for years by political actors, including government officials, to discredit critics.

Hajjat also argues that the current government is "implementing a far-right agenda through the erosion of fundamental rights and freedoms - including the rights to association, protest and expression - and through the brutal repression of political dissent".

The French Human Rights League (LDH) regularly describes as "liberty-restricting" the laws and legislative proposals that expand police powers, extend mass surveillance, curb the right to protest or target minorities and civil society organisations in France.

Among them is the law on the presumption of self-defence passed by the National Assembly in July. Nicknamed the "licence to kill law" by the LDH, it eases the conditions under which law enforcement officers may claim self-defence.

The organisation has also consistently criticised the 2021 so-called anti-separatism law, arguing that it fosters a climate of suspicion directed at Muslims.

Meanwhile, Amnesty International has warned about the violent policing of recent demonstrations, including the use of weapons capable of causing permanent injuries.

Since the protests began in September, thousands of people have been arrested across France on grounds ranging from public-order offences to damage to public and private property. Eighty-five percent of those taken into custody are minors.

Mounting attacks on the left

In the aftermath of the violence that erupted during the 17 October demonstrations, Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin called for exceptional legal measures, including treating certain acts as organised crime offences and applying some tools normally associated with anti-terrorism legislation.

The minister specifically highlighted the role of the "ultra left" and the "far left" in the violence and looting.

‘Claiming that LFI raises issues such as racism and support for the Palestinian people merely to court Muslim voters is part of this broader effort to discredit the party’

- Jeremy Younes, researcher at media watchdog Acrimed

He claimed that presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon and his party France Unbowed (LFI), which was classified as far left in a February ministerial circular, bore "part of the responsibility" for the violence surrounding the demonstrations.

Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu likewise accused LFI of "fuelling anger".

The accusation enjoys broad support among Macron's centrist coalition, the traditional right and the far right. Even Socialist Party candidate Raphael Glucksmann, accused by parts of the left of being out of touch with the working classes and an obstacle to left-wing unity, has accused Melenchon of "brutalising public debate".

Yet according to French intelligence services, traditional left-wing parties such as LFI and the Communist Party, although present at demonstrations, were not involved in the violence.

An investigation by Mediapart further revealed that internal intelligence reports contradicted the government's political narrative. Some officers reportedly said they were pressured to blame LFI for violence that the party did not instigate during the 17 October protests

For LFI leaders, who accuse the government of manipulation, these revelations illustrate a broader effort to demonise the party.

Jeremy Younes, a researcher at media watchdog Acrimed, shares the view that the party of Melenchon - who is currently projected by some polls to face Le Pen in the second round of the election - is the target of a delegitimisation campaign by both the media and the political establishment.

"Since its creation in 2016, LFI has faced hostility from journalists and commentators largely because it broke with the neoliberal consensus and adopted anti-racist positions that have led to it being labelled 'Islamo-leftist'," he told MEE.

In France, most major private media outlets are owned by a handful of billionaires and large industrial or financial groups opposed to key elements of the party's programme, including proposals for wealth redistribution and the dismantling of private media empires to increase pluralism.

Younes describes media coverage of LFI as a constant barrage of attacks, denouncing what he sees as a systematic effort to exclude the movement from the republican mainstream through endless controversy rather than substantive debate about policies and facts.

"Claiming that LFI raises issues such as racism and support for the Palestinian people merely to court Muslim voters is part of this broader effort to discredit the party," he said. "The conditions under which the left can express itself are being undermined everywhere."

France: Far-right party’s ‘de‑demonisation’ strategy rattled by antisemitism scandal
Read More »

One media outlet stands out in what critics call "LFI-bashing": CNews. Described by Reporters Without Borders as a far-right opinion channel, the rolling-news station is currently the target of a petition calling for it to lose its broadcasting licence. The petition has gathered close to one million signatures, constitutionally opening the way for a parliamentary review.

An online campaign is also encouraging French social media users to reduce the visibility of content promoting far-right narratives.

According to Sopo, such initiatives "can play a useful role". He believes that "a civic awakening committed to building a society based on coexistence is necessary".

However, he added: "Today, society is so polarised that it is difficult for an anti-racist movement to build broad public support."

For Hajjat, if the National Rally comes to power, "it would already have all the legislation necessary to implement its racist, sexist, homophobic and anti-social programme”.

The academic argues that the normalisation of far-right ideas, and their gradual incorporation into law by the current administration, are paving the way for the victory of Le Pen, who remains the clear frontrunner in voting-intention polls.

If she wins the election, Hajjat warned, “foreign nationals and French citizens of immigrant origin would be the first targets of legal discrimination in areas including housing, employment and education among others."
